claim: Tet2 and Tet3 mRNAs are abundantly expressed at all stages of B cell development, whereas Tet1 mRNA is expressed at much lower levels.
source: Tet2 and Tet3 mRNAs are abundantly expressed at all stages of B cell development, whereas Tet1 mRNA is expressed at much lower levels (Ko et al., 2010)(Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, left, blue bars).
evidence: Supported by reference to published data (Ko et al., 2010) and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Neither Tet2-/- mice nor Tet3fl/fl Mb1Cre mice displayed any striking B cell phenotypes.
source: However neither Tet2-/- mice (which are fully viable and fertile [Ko et al., 2011]) nor Tet3fl/fl Mb1Cre mice (which we generated to bypass the perinatal lethality of Tet3-/- mice [Gu et al., 2011]) displayed any striking B cell phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C and D and not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C and D, and citations to Ko et al., 2011 and Gu et al., 2011

claim: 5hmC levels were at least 4-fold lower in vitro-cultured pro-B cells of Tet2/3 DKO mice compared to wild type.
source: As judged by DNA dot blot using an anti-5hmC antibody, 5hmC levels were at least 4-fold lower in vitro-cultured pro-B cells of Tet2/3 DKO mice compared to wild type (WT) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, right).
evidence: Supported by DNA dot blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Tet2/3 DKO mice showed a striking reduction in the percentages and numbers of B cells in the bone marrow compared to WT mice, with a partial block at the pro-B to pre-B transition.
source: Tet2/3 DKO mice showed a striking reduction in the percentages and numbers of B cells in the bone marrow compared to WT mice, with a partial block at the pro-B to pre-B transition (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1

claim: The percentage of B220+CD19+ cells in the Tet2/3 DKO bone marrow was substantially reduced (<50% of that in WT bone marrow) at 7–8 weeks and even more pronounced (<10%) at 11–12 weeks of age.
source: The percentage of B220+CD19+ cells in the Tet2/3 DKO bone marrow was substantially reduced (<50% of that in WT bone marrow) at 7–8 weeks and even more pronounced (<10%) at 11–12 weeks of age (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The percentages and numbers of pre-B cells and immature B cells in the Tet2/3 DKO bone marrow at 11–12 weeks were 7–20% of those in the WT bone marrow.
source: The percentages and numbers of pre-B cells (CD43lowB220+IgM-) and immature B cells (CD43lowB220+IgM+) in the Tet2/3 DKO bone marrow at 11–12 weeks were 7–20% of those in the WT bone marrow (Figure 1B–D)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B-D

claim: The percentages and numbers of re-circulating (mature) IgM+IgD+CD19+ B cells in the bone marrow were greatly diminished in Tet2/3 DKO mice.
source: concomitantly, the percentages and numbers of re-circulating (mature) IgM+IgD+CD19+ B cells in the bone marrow were also greatly diminished in Tet2/3 DKO mice (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and 1D

claim: Tet2/3 DKO mice showed an increased percentage of pro-B cells in the bone marrow, but total pro-B cell numbers were unaltered.
source: In parallel, Tet2/3 DKO mice showed an increased percentage of pro-B cells (IgM-CD19+B220+ckit+CD25–) in the bone marrow (Figure 1E, left), but total pro-B cell numbers were unaltered because of the overall decrease in total B-lineage cells (Figure 1E, right).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E

claim: There was a reduction in the percentage and number of mature B cells in the spleen of Tet2/3 DKO mice.
source: Consistent with these findings, there was a reduction in the percentage and number of mature B cells in the spleen (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F

claim: A large fraction of CD19+B220+ B cells in the spleen of Tet2/3 DKO mice lacked cell-surface IgM and/or IgD expression (~25% and~45% IgM–IgD– cells in eight week-old and 11 week-old Tet2/3 DKO mice respectively).
source: A large fraction of CD19+B220+ B cells in the spleen of Tet2/3 DKO mice lacked cell-surface IgM and/or IgD expression (~25% and~45% IgM–IgD– cells in eight week-old and 11 week-old Tet2/3 DKO mice respectively; Figure 1G)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Peripheral Ig-negative B cells in Tet2/3 DKO mice expressed a significantly higher level of Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and pre-BCR (VpreB).
source: These peripheral Ig-negative B cells expressed a significantly higher level of Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and pre-BCR (VpreB, also known as CD179α), thus displaying the expression profile of developing pro-B cells (Figure 1H)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H

claim: Peripheral Ig-negative B cells in Tet2/3 DKO mice uniformly lacked expression of Tet3 mRNA, indicating complete deletion of the Tet3 allele.
source: they also uniformly lacked expression of Tet3 mRNA, indicating complete deletion of the Tet3 allele (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: Two out of 3 surface Ig-positive cell samples from Tet2/3 DKO mice showed residual expression of Tet3 mRNA.
source: In contrast, two out of 3 surface Ig-positive cell samples analyzed showed residual expression of Tet3 mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: There was a detectable expansion of CD11b+ myeloid-lineage cells in the bone marrow and spleen of Tet2/3 DKO mice.
source: Notably, there was a detectable expansion of CD11b+ myeloid-lineage cells in the bone marrow and spleen of Tet2/3 DKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), resembling the myeloid skewing observed in mice deficient in Tet2 or Tet3 alone in the hematopoietic compartment (Ko et al., 2011, 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and citations to Ko et al., 2011, 2015

claim: All older Tet2/3 DKO mice developed B cell lymphomas with splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy by the time they were five months old.
source: Moreover, all older Tet2/3 DKO mice developed B cell lymphomas with splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy by the time they were five months old (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: Splenic Tet2/3 DKO B cells that lacked cell-surface IgM and/or IgD expression showed greatly reduced expression of cell-surface and intracellular Igκ light chains.
source: The splenic Tet2/3 DKO B cells that lacked cell-surface IgM and/or IgD expression (Figure 1G) also showed greatly reduced expression of cell-surface and intracellular Igκ light chains (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Splenic Tet2/3 DKO B cells that lacked cell-surface IgM and/or IgD expression showed impaired Igκ rearrangement.
source: The splenic Tet2/3 DKO B cells that lacked cell-surface IgM and/or IgD expression (Figure 1G) also showed greatly reduced expression of cell-surface and intracellular Igκ light chains (Figure 2A) and impaired Igκ rearrangement (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by PCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Purified pre-B cells from Tet2/3 DKO mice showed a marked reduction (>50%) in Vκ-Jκ1 rearrangement compared to their WT counterparts.
source: Furthermore, purified pre-B cells from Tet2/3 DKO mice showed a marked reduction (>50%) in Vκ-Jκ1 rearrangement compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C

claim: TET function is important for Igκ locus rearrangement and κ chain expression in developing B cells.
source: Furthermore, purified pre-B cells from Tet2/3 DKO mice showed a marked reduction (>50%) in Vκ-Jκ1 rearrangement compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 2C), demonstrating that TET function is important for Igκ locus rearrangement and κ chain expression in developing B cells and hence critical for the generation of mature B cells with functional B cell receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing reduced Igκ rearrangement in Tet2/3 DKO mice

claim: All 5 CpG sites in the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers were fully 'methylated' (5mC + 5hmC) in LSK cells.
source: Using bisulfite sequencing (which does not distinguish 5hmC from 5mC, or 5fC and 5caC from unmodified C [Huang et al., 2010; Pastor et al., 2013]), we found that all 5 CpG sites in the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers were fully 'methylated' (5mC + 5 hmC) in LSK (Lin-, Sca1+ c-kit+) cells, a population enriched in hematopoietic stem/precursor (HSPC) cells (Hodges et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data and citations to Huang et al., 2010; Pastor et al., 2013; Hodges et al., 2011

claim: CpG sites in the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers began to lose methylation at the pre-pro-B cell stage, were partially methylated in pro-B cells, and almost completely 'unmethylated' in WT splenic CD19+ B cells.
source: we found that all 5 CpG sites in the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers were fully 'methylated' (5mC + 5 hmC) in LSK (Lin-, Sca1+ c-kit+) cells, a population enriched in hematopoietic stem/precursor (HSPC) cells (Hodges et al., 2011); began to lose this modification at the pre-pro-B cell stage; were partially methylated in pro-B cells; and almost completely 'unmethylated' (C/5fC/5caC) in WT splenic CD19+ B cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The corresponding human Igκ enhancers undergo B cell-specific 'demethylation' (loss of 5mC/5hmC).
source: Examination of publicly available data for human HSC, neutrophils and B cells showed that the corresponding human enhancers also undergo B cell-specific 'demethylation' (loss of 5mC/5hmC; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by publicly available data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: In vitro-generated Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells displayed a striking increase in DNA modification (5mC + 5hmC) at the 3' and distal Igκ enhancers compared to control pro-B cells.
source: Bisulfite sequencing showed that in vitro-generated Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells displayed a striking increase in DNA modification (5mC + 5 hmC) at the 3' and distal Igκ enhancers and a parallel decrease (>90%) in Cκ transcripts and Igκ germline (GL) transcripts compared to control pro-B cells (Figure 3C and D, compare blue and green bars)
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 3C and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D

claim: In vitro-generated Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells showed a parallel decrease (>90%) in Cκ transcripts and Igκ germline (GL) transcripts compared to control pro-B cells.
source: Bisulfite sequencing showed that in vitro-generated Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells displayed a striking increase in DNA modification (5mC + 5 hmC) at the 3' and distal Igκ enhancers and a parallel decrease (>90%) in Cκ transcripts and Igκ germline (GL) transcripts compared to control pro-B cells (Figure 3C and D, compare blue and green bars)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The increased modification in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells reflected increased DNA methylation (5mC, not 5hmC), since genome-wide 5hmC mapping by CMS-IP showed almost no remaining 5hmC in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells compared to WT pro-B cells.
source: The increased modification indeed reflected increased DNA methylation (5mC, not 5hmC), since genome-wide 5hmC mapping by CMS-IP showed almost no remaining 5hmC in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells compared to WT pro-B cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by CMS-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: In vitro-generated pro-B cells deficient in Tet2 alone showed a partial increase in methylation and a partial reduction in Cκ and Igκ germline transcripts.
source: In vitro-generated pro-B cells deficient in Tet2 alone (Tet2-/-Tet3fl/fl cells transduced with empty retrovirus, Figure 3C-3E, red bars) showed a partial increase in methylation (Figure 3C) and a partial reduction in Cκ and Igκ germline transcripts (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: Loss of Tet2 in vivo had no apparent effect on methylation of Igκ enhancers.
source: whereas loss of Tet2 in vivo had no apparent effect (Figure 3E)
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Tet3 can compensate fully for lack of Tet2 in vivo but not in vitro.
source: suggesting redundant functions of Tet2 and Tet3 in modulating the DNA modification status of these Igκ enhancers and showing that Tet3 can compensate fully for lack of Tet2 in vivo but not in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of Tet2 alone has no effect in vivo but partial effect in vitro

claim: Igκ germline transcription and Igκ rearrangement is regulated by the concerted action of multiple transcription factors at the Eκ enhancers, including E2A, EBF1, PAX5, PU.1, IRF4 and IRF8.
source: Igκ germline transcription and Igκ rearrangement is regulated by the concerted action of multiple transcription factors at the Eκ enhancers, including E2A, EBF1, PAX5, PU.1, IRF4 and IRF8 (Clark et al., 2014; Cobaleda et al., 2007; Hagman and Lukin, 2006; Murre, 2005)(Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2014; Cobaleda et al., 2007; Hagman and Lukin, 2006; Murre, 2005

claim: With the exception of IRF4 and IRF8, mRNA and protein levels for most known regulators of Igκ were unchanged in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells compared to WT.
source: With the exception of the functionally redundant transcription factors IRF4 and IRF8 which showed decreased expression (see below), mRNA and protein levels for most of these known regulators were unchanged in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells compared to WT (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and not shown).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Tet2/3 DKO pre-B cells transformed with BCR-ABL had diminished Igκ germline transcription, both under resting conditions and after treatment with Gleevec.
source: Similarly, Tet2/3 DKO pre-B cells transformed with BCR-ABL (Chen et al., 1994; Klug et al., 1994) had diminished Igκ germline transcription, both under resting conditions and after treatment with the Abelson kinase inhibitor Gleevec (also known as imatinib or STI-571), which induces Igκ locus activation in BCR-Abl-transformed cells (Muljo and Schlissel, 2003) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and citations to Chen et al., 1994; Klug et al., 1994; Muljo and Schlissel, 2003

claim: Gleevec-treated Tet2/3 DKO pre-B cells had significantly reduced formation of Rag-induced DNA double-strand breaks at the Jκ1 segment compared to WT cells.
source: Gleevec-treated Tet2/3 DKO pre-B cells also had significantly reduced formation of Rag-induced DNA double-strand breaks at the Jκ1 segment compared to WT cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by ligation-mediated PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E

claim: TET proteins demethylate and modulate the activity of Igκ enhancers and thus influence subsequent Igκ rearrangement.
source: These results show that TET proteins demethylate and modulate the activity of Igκ enhancers and thus influence subsequent Igκ rearrangement.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing increased methylation and decreased rearrangement in Tet2/3 DKO cells

claim: 1303 regions (2.2%) were more accessible in WT than in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells (WT>DKO differentially accessible regions).
source: Importantly, 1303 regions (2.2%) were potentially regulated by TET because they were more accessible in WT than in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells (Figure 4A, WT>DKO differentially accessible regions (WT>DKO DARs); blue dots).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4A

claim: 1192 regions (2.1%) gained accessibility in the Tet2/3 DKO cells (DKO>WT differentially accessible regions).
source: 1192 regions (2.1%) gained accessibility in the Tet2/3 DKO cells (Figure 4A, DKO>WT differentially accessible regions (DKO>WT DARs); red dots), and are likely affected indirectly by TET (see below).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4A

claim: All accessible regions displayed higher levels of 5hmC compared to randomly sampled regions, suggesting an overall positive correlation between TET activity (5hmC deposition) and chromatin accessibility.
source: Compared to randomly sampled regions (Figure 4B, dotted line), all accessible regions displayed higher levels of 5hmC (solid lines), suggesting an overall positive correlation between TET activity (5hmC deposition) and chromatin accessibility.
evidence: Supported by CMS-IP data shown in Figure 4B

claim: DARs that were more accessible in WT than in DKO pro-B cells (TET-regulated DARs) exhibited significantly higher levels of 5hmC compared to other accessible regions.
source: DARs that were more accessible in WT than in DKO pro-B cells (TET-regulated DARs, WT>DKO DARs or simply, WT DARs) exhibited significantly higher levels of 5hmC compared to other accessible regions (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by CMS-IP data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The majority (>86%) of TET-regulated DARs exhibit the characteristics of enhancers: they are located distal to transcription start sites and are enriched for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3.
source: The majority (>86%) of TET-regulated DARs exhibit the characteristics of enhancers: they are located distal to transcription start sites (Figure 4C) and are enriched for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3 (Creyghton et al., 2010; Shlyueva et al., 2014) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4D, and citations to Creyghton et al., 2010; Shlyueva et al., 2014

claim: TET deficiency greatly decreased the accessibility of the dEκ enhancer.
source: As expected from this global analysis, TET deficiency greatly decreased the accessibility of the dEκ enhancer (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The E-box/ basic region-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) (CANNTG) motif was highly represented in TET-regulated regions (WT>DKO DARs) compared to commonly accessible regions.
source: Comparing TET-regulated regions (WT>DKO DARs) to commonly accessible regions, the E-box/ basic region-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) (CANNTG) motif was highly represented, with the second most prominent motif being the composite ETS:IRF (PU.1-IRF) motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The composite ETS:IRF (PU.1-IRF) motif was the second most prominent motif in TET-regulated regions (WT>DKO DARs) compared to commonly accessible regions.
source: Comparing TET-regulated regions (WT>DKO DARs) to commonly accessible regions, the E-box/ basic region-helix-loop-helix (bHLH) (CANNTG) motif was highly represented, with the second most prominent motif being the composite ETS:IRF (PU.1-IRF) motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: WT>DKO DARs showed strong enrichment for PU.1 and E2A binding sites identified experimentally by ChIP-seq.
source: Consistent with their enrichment for bHLH and ETS binding motifs, WT>DKO DARs showed strong enrichment for PU.1 and E2A binding sites identified experimentally by ChIP-seq (Heinz et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010), compared to DARs more accessible in DKO than in WT, commonly accessible regions and control random regions (Figure 4F,G)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4F and 4G, and citations to Heinz et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010

claim: A fraction of the commonly accessible regions corresponded to regions with significant CTCF binding in pro-B cells, suggesting these regions are potent insulators.
source: Notably, consistent with a previous study (Benner et al., 2015), a fraction of the commonly accessible regions (especially those with the lowest ATAC-seq signals) corresponded to regions with significant CTCF binding in pro-B cells (Lin et al., 2010), suggesting these regions are potent insulators (Song et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data and citations to Benner et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2010; Song et al., 2011

claim: CTCF binding sites were not enriched in the WT>DKO and DKO>WT DARs.
source: In contrast, CTCF binding sites were not enriched in the WT>DKO and DKO>WT DARs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Regulation of insulator accessibility is likely TET-independent.
source: These results suggest that regulation of insulator accessibility is likely TET-independent and imply that multiple mechanisms exist to regulate accessibility in different chromatin contexts.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CTCF binding sites were not enriched in TET-regulated DARs

claim: 872 regions showed increased methylation and 258 showed decreased methylation in DKO pro-B cells compared to WT.
source: Analysis of these differentially methylated regions (DMRs) showed that DMRs with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (DKO>WT DMRs) were concurrently less accessible (Figure 5A, left; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, compare first and second columns), and had originally been modified with 5hmC in WT pro-B cells (Figure 5A, right; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, see third column), suggesting that TET activity is required for antagonizing DNA methylation and maintaining accessibility at these regions.
evidence: Supported by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data

claim: DMRs with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT were concurrently less accessible.
source: Analysis of these differentially methylated regions (DMRs) showed that DMRs with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (DKO>WT DMRs) were concurrently less accessible (Figure 5A, left; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, compare first and second columns)
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and WGBS data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: DMRs with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT had originally been modified with 5hmC in WT pro-B cells.
source: Analysis of these differentially methylated regions (DMRs) showed that DMRs with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (DKO>WT DMRs) were concurrently less accessible (Figure 5A, left; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, compare first and second columns), and had originally been modified with 5hmC in WT pro-B cells (Figure 5A, right; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, see third column)
evidence: Supported by CMS-IP data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: TET activity is required for antagonizing DNA methylation and maintaining accessibility at regions with increased methylation in DKO cells.
source: Analysis of these differentially methylated regions (DMRs) showed that DMRs with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (DKO>WT DMRs) were concurrently less accessible (Figure 5A, left; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, compare first and second columns), and had originally been modified with 5hmC in WT pro-B cells (Figure 5A, right; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, see third column), suggesting that TET activity is required for antagonizing DNA methylation and maintaining accessibility at these regions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that regions with increased methylation in DKO were less accessible and had 5hmC in WT

claim: The majority of regions with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (72.5%) show characteristics of enhancers: location distal to transcription start sites and relative enrichment for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3.
source: Consistent with the role of TET in regulating enhancer accessibility (shown above), the majority of regions with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (72.5%) show characteristics of enhancers: location distal to transcription start sites (Figure 5B) and relative enrichment for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3 (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B and 5C

claim: Regions with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT were enriched for E2A and PU.1 binding.
source: the majority of regions with increased methylation in DKO cells compared to WT (72.5%) show characteristics of enhancers: location distal to transcription start sites (Figure 5B) and relative enrichment for H3K4me1 over H3K4me3 (Figure 5C) and were enriched for E2A and PU.1 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; compared to randomly sampled regions in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B

claim: There is a strong correlation between chromatin accessibility, TET enzymatic activity based on generation of 5hmC, and maintenance of DNA demethylation at the enhancer regions marked by 5hmC.
source: Together these results emphasize the strong correlation between chromatin accessibility, TET enzymatic activity based on generation of 5hmC, and maintenance of DNA demethylation at the enhancer regions marked by 5hmC.
evidence: Inferred from the combined ATAC-seq, CMS-IP, and WGBS data

claim: Depletion of E2A increased the average level of DNA methylation at the first and second CpGs of the distal Eκ enhancer by 2- to 3-fold.
source: The shRNAs reduced the amount of E2A and PU.1 proteins substantially (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), and increased the average level of DNA methylation at the first and second CpGs of the distal Eκ enhancer by 2- to 3-fold (Figure 6A and B), a magnitude similar to that observed in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Depletion of PU.1 increased the average level of DNA methylation at the first and second CpGs of the distal Eκ enhancer by 2- to 3-fold.
source: The shRNAs reduced the amount of E2A and PU.1 proteins substantially (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), and increased the average level of DNA methylation at the first and second CpGs of the distal Eκ enhancer by 2- to 3-fold (Figure 6A and B), a magnitude similar to that observed in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6B

claim: TET2 co-immunoprecipitated with E2A and PU.1.
source: We found that indeed, TET2 co-immunoprecipitated with E2A and PU.1 (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The interaction between TET2 and E2A/PU.1 was direct, since benzonase and ethidium bromide were used to prevent false positive interactions indirectly mediated by contaminating nucleic acids.
source: the interaction was direct, since we used benzonase (a nuclease that degrades both DNA and RNA) and the DNA intercalator ethidium bromide to prevent false positive interactions indirectly mediated by contaminating nucleic acids in cell extracts.
evidence: Supported by the experimental design using benzonase and ethidium bromide

claim: E2A and PU.1 recruit TET proteins to enhancers, where they increase chromatin accessibility by depositing 5hmC and facilitating DNA demethylation.
source: These findings suggested that E2A and PU.1 recruit TET proteins to enhancers, where they increase chromatin accessibility by depositing 5hmC and facilitating DNA demethylation.
evidence: Inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data and the functional data showing increased methylation upon E2A/PU.1 depletion

claim: Recruitment of TET proteins to the distal Eκ enhancer was significantly diminished in cells depleted for either E2A or PU.1.
source: Indeed, recruitment of TET proteins to the distal Eκ enhancer was significantly diminished in cells depleted for either E2A or PU.1 (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and 6E

claim: Recruitment of TET2 to the 3'Eκ enhancer was not significantly affected by depletion of E2A or PU.1.
source: Notably, recruitment of TET2 to the 3'Eκ enhancer was not significantly affected (Figure 6D and E)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and 6E

claim: The genome-wide binding of PU.1 was virtually indistinguishable between WT and Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that the genome-wide binding of PU.1 was virtually indistinguishable between WT and Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: PU.1 is upstream of TET and enlists TET activity to modulate the accessibility of bound enhancers.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that the genome-wide binding of PU.1 was virtually indistinguishable between WT and Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that PU.1 is upstream of TET and enlists TET activity to modulate the accessibility of bound enhancers.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PU.1 binding is unchanged in Tet2/3 DKO cells

claim: Tet2/3 DKO BCR-Abl pre-B cells reconstituted with catalytically-active Tet2CD showed increased Igκ germline and IgCκ transcription.
source: Under these conditions, Tet2/3 DKO BCR-Abl pre-B cells reconstituted with catalytically-active Tet2CD showed increased Igκ germline and IgCκ transcription (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Tet2/3 DKO BCR-Abl pre-B cells reconstituted with catalytically-active Tet2CD displayed decreased DNA methylation at the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers, compared to mock-transduced cells.
source: they also displayed decreased DNA methylation at the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers, compared to mock-transduced cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Cells transduced with a catalytically-inactive version of Tet2CD (HxD mutant) were functionally inert.
source: Cells transduced with a catalytically-inactive version of Tet2CD (HxD mutant (Ko et al., 2010; Tahiliani et al., 2009) were functionally inert (Figure 7B and C)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 7B and 7C, and citations to Ko et al., 2010; Tahiliani et al., 2009

claim: The catalytically-inactive Tet2CD HxD mutant protein was recruited to the 3' Eκ and distal Eκ enhancers as or almost as effectively as the catalytically active version.
source: despite the fact that the mutant protein was recruited to the 3' Eκ and distal Eκ enhancers as or almost as effectively as the catalytically active version (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Expression of Tet2CD, but not its HxD mutant, restored chromatin accessibility at the 3'Eκ and distal Eκ enhancers in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
source: Expression of Tet2CD, but not its HxD mutant, also restored chromatin accessibility at the 3'Eκ and distal Eκ enhancers (Figure 7E) as well as at a genome-wide level (Figure 7F) in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 7E and 7F

claim: Re-expression of Tet2CD was able to restore the VκJ rearrangement in Tet2/3 DKO pre-B cells.
source: Importantly, re-expression of Tet2CD was able to restore the VκJ rearrangement in Tet2/3 DKO pre-B cells (Figure 7G), demonstrating the functional relevance of enhancer accessibility to biological outcome.
evidence: Supported by ligation-mediated-PCR data shown in Figure 7G

claim: Tet2/3 DKO cells showed a significant decrease in Irf4 mRNA and protein levels.
source: In addition to decreased levels of Igκ germline transcripts, Tet2/3 DKO cells showed a significant decrease in Irf4 mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Expression of IRF4 protein and mRNA required TET catalytic activity, since re-expression of Tet2CD restored mRNA and protein levels of IRF4 whereas the Tet2CDHxD mutant did not.
source: Expression of IRF4 protein and mRNA required TET catalytic activity, since re-expression of Tet2CD restored mRNA and protein levels of IRF4 whereas the Tet2CDHxD mutant did not (Figures 7B and 8A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 8A

claim: TET2 and TET3 proteins are required for the expression of IRF4 and, to a lesser extent, IRF8.
source: Our data show that in addition to regulating Igκ germline transcription, TET2 and TET3 proteins are required for the expression of IRF4 and, to a lesser extent, IRF8.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing decreased IRF4 and IRF8 expression in Tet2/3 DKO cells

claim: Over-expression of IRF4 marginally induced Igκ gene transcription and did not affect 3'Eκ and dEκ methylation in the absence of TET.
source: Nonetheless, over-expression of IRF4 marginally induced Igκ gene transcription and did not affect 3'Eκ and dEκ methylation in the absence of TET (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8B and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 8C

claim: IRF4 is induced via TET catalytic activity and then functions downstream of TET proteins in regulating early B cell development.
source: These results suggested that IRF4 is induced via TET catalytic activity and then functions downstream of TET proteins in regulating early B cell development.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TET is required for IRF4 expression but IRF4 cannot rescue TET deficiency

claim: Mice with a germline deletion of Tet2 in conjunction with Mb1Cre-driven deletion of Tet3 display a block in B cell development at the pro-B to pre-B transition, reflective of decreased Igκ rearrangement and expression.
source: We have shown that mice with a germline deletion of Tet2 in conjunction with Mb1Cre-driven deletion of Tet3 display a block in B cell development at the pro-B to pre-B transition, reflective of decreased Igκ rearrangement and expression.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: A profound loss of TET function is necessary for B cell developmental defects, since mice lacking only Tet2 or Tet3 in B cells have no obvious B cell phenotypes.
source: A profound loss of TET function is necessary, since mice lacking only Tet2 or Tet3 in B cells have no obvious B cell phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by the observation that single knockouts have no phenotype while double knockout does

claim: TET proteins concurrently regulate Igκ germline transcription and the DNA methylation status of the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers, through a mechanism that requires TET catalytic activity.
source: By acute Cre-mediated deletion of Tet3 in cultured pro-B cells and rescue with Tet2, we have demonstrated that TET proteins concurrently regulate Igκ germline transcription and the DNA methylation status of the 3' and distal Eκ enhancers, through a mechanism that requires TET catalytic activity.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data showing rescue with catalytically active but not inactive Tet2CD

claim: Conditional Dnmt3a/b deletion results in early Vκ-Jκ rearrangement, increased expression of Igκ germline transcripts, and decreased DNA methylation at Igκ enhancers.
source: Moreover, conditional Dnmt3a/b deletion results in early Vκ-Jκ rearrangement, increased expression of Igκ germline transcripts, and decreased DNA methylation at Igκ enhancers (Manoharan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manoharan et al., 2015

claim: Tet2 and Tet3 maintain chromatin accessibility at Igκ locus enhancers as well as at many other promoters and enhancers in pro-B cells.
source: Our data suggest that Tet2 and Tet3 maintain chromatin accessibility at Igκ locus enhancers as well as at many other promoters and enhancers in pro-B cells.
evidence: Supported by the ATAC-seq data showing decreased accessibility at multiple regions in Tet2/3 DKO cells

claim: The TET enzymatic activity has a primary and essential role in maintaining chromatin accessibility.
source: While many protein complexes can modulate chromatin accessibility, the fact that acute deletion of TET function almost eliminates Igκ germline transcription, in a manner that can be rescued by a TET catalytic domain, implies that the TET enzymatic activity has a primary and essential role.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing that catalytic activity is required

claim: Genomic regions that are less accessible in Tet2/3 DKO compared to WT pro-B cells are enriched for E2A and PU.1 binding motifs.
source: We have shown that genomic regions that are less accessible in Tet2/3 DKO compared to WT pro-B cells are enriched for E2A and PU.1 binding motifs
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis

claim: A subset of validated E2A and PU.1 binding sites, including the Igκ enhancers, are less accessible in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
source: and conversely, a subset of validated E2A and PU.1 binding sites, including the Igκ enhancers, are less accessible in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data

claim: Both E2A and PU.1 transcription factors are involved in maintaining the demethylated status of the distal Eκ enhancer.
source: Notably, both transcription factors are involved in maintaining the demethylated status of the distal Eκ enhancer.
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing increased methylation upon E2A or PU.1 depletion

claim: PU.1 functions in macrophages as a 'pioneer' transcription factor capable of enhancing chromatin accessibility by binding linker regions between nucleosomes.
source: PU.1, a key transcription factor in both the myeloid and lymphoid lineages, functions in macrophages as a 'pioneer' transcription factor capable of enhancing chromatin accessibility by binding linker regions between nucleosomes, thereby facilitating the modification of neighboring histones and the binding of other transcription factors (Ghisletti et al., 2010; Heinz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghisletti et al., 2010; Heinz et al., 2010

claim: Both TET2 and DNMT3b co-immunoprecipitate with PU.1 in macrophages.
source: Consistent with a previous finding in macrophages that both TET2 and DNMT3b co-immunoprecipitate with PU.1 (de la Rica et al., 2013), we report here that TET2 co-immunoprecipitates with both PU.1 and E2A in developing B cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to de la Rica et al., 2013

claim: Loss of TET2 and TET3 has a limited effect on the binding of PU.1.
source: Loss of TET2 and TET3 has a limited effect on the binding of PU.1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: PU.1, and potentially E2A, recruit TET proteins to Igκ and other enhancers where they render the enhancers permissive for additional and/or more stable binding of those and other transcription factors.
source: suggesting that PU.1, and potentially E2A, recruit TET proteins to Igκ and other enhancers where they render the enhancers permissive for additional and/or more stable binding of those and other transcription factors (Figure 8D).
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on TET recruitment, DNA methylation, and chromatin accessibility

claim: IRF4 and IRF8 are functionally redundant for the rearrangement of Ig light chains during pro-B to pre-B transition.
source: IRF4 and IRF8 are functionally redundant for the rearrangement of Ig light chains during pro-B to pre-B transition (Lu et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2003

claim: EBF1 is imperative for the pre-pro-B to pro-B transition.
source: while EBF1 is imperative for the pre-pro-B to pro-B transition (Lin and Grosschedl, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin and Grosschedl, 1995

claim: Ectopic IRF4 expression induced Igκ germline transcription as well as premature Igκ rearrangement in WT pro-B cells.
source: Ectopic IRF4 expression induced Igκ germline transcription as well as premature Igκ rearrangement in WT pro-B cells (Bevington and Boyes, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bevington and Boyes, 2013

claim: Ectopic expression of IRF4 in Tet2/3 DKO cells only marginally increased Igκ germline transcription.
source: but ectopic expression of IRF4 in Tet2/3 DKO cells only marginally increased Igκ germline transcription.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Expression of IRF4 in Tet2/3 DKO cells had no effect on the DNA modification status of the Igκ enhancers.
source: Moreover, expression of IRF4 in Tet2/3 DKO cells had no effect on the DNA modification status of the Igκ enhancers
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 8C

claim: IRF4 and IRF8 function at a late stage, after transcription factors such as PU.1 and E2A have cooperated with TET enzymes to facilitate enhancer accessibility.
source: suggesting that IRF4 and IRF8 function at a late stage, after transcription factors such as PU.1 and E2A have cooperated with TET enzymes to facilitate enhancer accessibility.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IRF4 cannot rescue TET deficiency

claim: CpG dinucleotides are present in at least one potential IRF4 binding site in both the 3'Eκ and dEκ enhancers.
source: Interestingly, CpG dinucleotides are present in at least one potential IRF4 binding site in both the 3'Eκ and dEκ enhancers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: TET-mediated demethylation may be required for efficient binding of IRF4 at the Igκ enhancers.
source: hinting that TET-mediated demethylation may be required for efficient binding of IRF4 at these enhancers.
evidence: Speculated based on the presence of CpG dinucleotides in IRF4 binding sites

claim: EBF1 has been shown to increase both chromatin accessibility and DNA demethylation in B progenitor cells.
source: EBF1 has been shown to increase both chromatin accessibility and DNA demethylation in B progenitor cells (Boller et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Boller et al., 2016

claim: EBF1 interacts with TET2 in a cancer cell line.
source: and to interact with TET2 in a cancer cell line (Guilhamon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guilhamon et al., 2013

claim: TET-mediated changes in DNA modification status and chromatin accessibility can be rescued by re-expression of the TET2 catalytic domain in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
source: Our reconstitution experiments show clearly that TET-mediated changes in DNA modification status and chromatin accessibility can be rescued by re-expression of the TET2 catalytic domain in Tet2/3 DKO pro-B cells.
evidence: Supported by the rescue experiments shown in Figure 7

claim: Many documented interactions of TET proteins with their partners involve the catalytic domain.
source: many documented interactions of TET proteins with their partners involve the catalytic domain (e.g. TET1-OGT (Balasubramani and Rao, 2013), TET2-IDAX (Ko et al., 2013))
evidence: Supported by citations to Balasubramani and Rao, 2013; Ko et al., 2013

claim: Tet2 lacks a covalently associated CXXC domain that would be expected to target it to genomic regions containing unmethylated CpGs.
source: and Tet2 lacks a covalently associated CXXC domain that would be expected to target it to genomic regions containing unmethylated CpGs (Ko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ko et al., 2013

claim: TET proteins have a role in mature B cells.
source: Our current study focuses on the function of Tet2 and Tet3 in early B cell development, but our data indicate that TET proteins also have a role in mature B cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of age-related decline of mature B cells in Tet2/3 DKO mice

claim: There was an age-related decline of mature B cells in Tet2/3 DKO mice, suggesting that Tet2 and Tet3 are important for B cell homeostasis.
source: Specifically, we observed an age-related decline of mature B cells in Tet2/3 DKO mice, suggesting that Tet2 and Tet3 are important for B cell homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by the flow cytometry data showing reduced mature B cells in older mice

claim: A fully penetrant development of B cell lymphomas occurred in all Tet2/3 DKO mice.
source: Despite this, we observed a fully penetrant development of B cell lymphomas in all Tet2/3 DKO mice
evidence: Supported by the observation that all older Tet2/3 DKO mice developed lymphomas

claim: Acute deletion of Tet2 and Tet3 in hematopoietic stem/precursor cells results in acute myeloid leukemia.
source: consistent with our recent finding that acute deletion of Tet2 and Tet3 in hematopoietic stem/ precursor cells results in acute myeloid leukemia (An et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to An et al., 2015

claim: Germline Tet1-deficient mice develop late B cell malignancies.
source: The data recall the late B cell malignancies observed in germline Tet1-deficient mice (Cimmino et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cimmino et al., 2015

claim: TET loss-of-function is associated with hematopoietic malignancies.
source: and reinforce the notion that TET loss-of-function is associated with hematopoietic malignancies (Huang and Rao, 2014; Ko et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang and Rao, 2014; Ko et al., 2015

claim: A recent study characterizing DNA methylation dynamics during human B cell differentiation revealed distinct demethylation patterns between early B cells and mature B cells.
source: A recent study characterizing DNA methylation dynamics during human B cell differentiation revealed distinct demethylation patterns between early B cells and mature B cells (Kulis et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kulis et al., 2015

claim: At least at Igκ enhancers in pro-B cells, the increase in DNA methylation that results from TET loss-of-function can be a determining ('instructive') factor for the observed decrease in Igκ germline transcription.
source: In contrast, our data suggest that at least at Igκ enhancers in pro-B cells, the increase in DNA methylation that results from TET loss-of-function can be a determining ('instructive') factor for the observed decrease in Igκ germline transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing that TET catalytic activity restores both demethylation and transcription

claim: Acute depletion of E2A results in increased DNA methylation at the distal Eκ enhancer, thus connecting transcription factor binding to DNA demethylation.
source: However, our data also show that acute depletion of E2A results in increased DNA methylation at the distal Eκ enhancer, thus connecting transcription factor binding to DNA demethylation as postulated (Bestor et al., 2015; Schübeler, 2015).
evidence: Supported by bisulfite sequencing data and citations to Bestor et al., 2015; Schübeler, 2015

claim: The simplest scenario is a positive feedback loop in which E2A, PU.1 and other transcription factors recruit TET proteins to enhancers, thus facilitating TET-mediated DNA modification; the recruited TET proteins, via DNA demethylation, maintain chromatin accessibility at these regions, promoting increased binding of E2A and other transcription factors such as PU.1.
source: The simplest scenario is a positive feedback loop in which E2A, PU.1 and other transcription factors (de la Rica et al., 2013; Guilhamon et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015) recruit TET proteins to enhancers, thus facilitating TET-mediated DNA modification; the recruited TET proteins, via DNA demethylation, maintain chromatin accessibility at these regions, promoting increased binding of E2A and other transcription factors such as PU.1 (Figure 8D).
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on TET recruitment, DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility, and transcription factor binding, with citations to de la Rica et al., 2013; Guilhamon et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015
